verses.text: Once again Jesus began to teach beside the sea, and such a large crowd gathered around Him that He got into a boat and sat in it, while all the people crowded along the shore.
And He taught them many things in parables, and in His teaching He said,
"Listen! A farmer went out to sow his seed.
And as he was sowing, some seed fell along the path, and the birds came and devoured it.
Some fell on rocky ground, where it did not have much soil. It sprang up quickly because the soil was shallow.
But when the sun rose, the seedlings were scorched, and they withered because they had no root.
Other seed fell among thorns, which grew up and choked the seedlings, and they yielded no crop.
Still other seed fell on good soil, where it sprouted, grew up, and produced a crop—one bearing thirtyfold, another sixtyfold, and another a hundredfold."
Then Jesus said, "He who has ears to hear, let him hear."
As soon as Jesus was alone with the Twelve and those around Him, they asked Him about the parable.
He replied, "The mystery of the kingdom of God has been given to you, but to those on the outside everything is expressed in parables,
so that, 'they may be ever seeing but never perceiving, and ever hearing but never understanding; otherwise they might turn and be forgiven.'"
Then Jesus said to them, "Do you not understand this parable? Then how will you understand any of the parables?
The farmer sows the word.
Some are like the seeds along the path, where the word is sown. As soon as they hear it, Satan comes and takes away the word that was sown in them.
Some are like the seeds sown on rocky ground. They hear the word and at once receive it with joy.
But they themselves have no root, and they remain for only a season. When trouble or persecution comes because of the word, they quickly fall away.
Others are like the seeds sown among the thorns. They hear the word,
but the worries of this life, the deceitfulness of wealth, and the desire for other things come in and choke the word, and it becomes unfruitful.
Still others are like the seeds sown on good soil. They hear the word, receive it, and produce a crop—thirtyfold, sixtyfold, or a hundredfold."
Jesus also said to them, "Does anyone bring in a lamp to put it under a basket or under a bed? Doesn't he set it on a stand?
For there is nothing hidden that will not be disclosed, and nothing concealed that will not be brought to light.
If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear."
He went on to say, "Pay attention to what you hear. With the measure you use, it will be measured to you, and even more will be added to you.
For whoever has will be given more. But whoever does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him."
Jesus also said, "The kingdom of God is like a man who scatters seed on the ground.
Night and day he sleeps and wakes, and the seed sprouts and grows, though he knows not how.
All by itself the earth produces a crop—first the stalk, then the head, then grain that ripens within.
And as soon as the grain is ripe, he swings the sickle, because the harvest has come."
Then He asked, "To what can we compare the kingdom of God? With what parable shall we present it?
It is like a mustard seed, which is the smallest of all seeds sown upon the earth.
But after it is planted, it grows to be the largest of all garden plants and puts forth great branches, so that the birds of the air nest in its shade."
With many such parables Jesus spoke the word to them, to the extent that they could understand.
He did not tell them anything without using a parable. But privately He explained everything to His own disciples.
When that evening came, He said to His disciples, "Let us cross to the other side."
After they had dismissed the crowd, they took Jesus with them, since He was already in the boat. And there were other boats with Him.
Soon a violent windstorm came up, and the waves were breaking over the boat, so that it was being swamped.
But Jesus was in the stern, sleeping on the cushion. So they woke Him and said, "Teacher, don't You care that we are perishing?"
Then Jesus got up and rebuked the wind and the sea. "Silence!" He commanded. "Be still!" And the wind died down, and it was perfectly calm.
"Why are you so afraid?" He asked. "Do you still have no faith?"
Overwhelmed with fear, they asked one another, "Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?"

context.author: Traditionally John Mark, a companion of Peter
context.genre: Teaching discourse — a connected block of parables about the kingdom of God, closing with a nature miracle that demonstrates the authority those parables describe
context.audience: Roman Christian readers, given both the public parables and the private explanation reserved only for Jesus' inner circle
context.setting: The Sea of Galilee's shoreline acts as a natural amphitheater, and teaching from a boat gave Jesus both distance from the crush of the crowd and a way for His voice to carry across the water to the shore.
context.custom: Galilean farmers scattered seed by hand before plowing, meaning some inevitably landed on hardened footpaths, thin soil over limestone shelf, or ground still thick with thornbush roots — every detail in the parable would have matched something the crowd could see from where they stood.
context.timelineImmediate: Mark groups several parables into one extended teaching session by the sea, then closes the chapter with the storm-calming miracle — pairing Jesus' words about the kingdom with a direct demonstration of the authority behind them.
context.timelineBible: Jesus' explanation for teaching in parables (v.12) directly quotes Isaiah 6:9-10, a passage originally describing Israel's spiritual dullness in Isaiah's own day — Jesus applies the same centuries-old diagnosis to His own generation.
context.sparkNotes: Jesus teaches an extended block of kingdom parables from a boat — the sower, the lamp, the growing seed, the mustard seed — then that evening calms a violent storm with two words: "Silence! Be still!" Mark notes Jesus explained everything privately to His own disciples but left the crowds with parables alone, a deliberate distinction Jesus grounds directly in Isaiah's centuries-old warning about seeing without perceiving.

translation.meaning: A comparison placed alongside a truth being taught — often a story from ordinary life used to illustrate something about the kingdom of God.

occurrences.note: Nearly all fifty uses cluster in the Synoptic Gospels around Jesus' own teaching — it appears only twice outside them, both in Hebrews.

translation.meaning: Divine secrets, previously hidden, now being disclosed — not permanently unknowable, but revealed selectively to those given ears to hear.
Mark's signature word, threading through this whole chapter of parables.

occurrences.note: The overwhelming majority of this word's New Testament uses are packed into Mark's sixteen short chapters alone.

gospelParallels.note: Matthew's fuller parallel collection of parables, including the sower, the weeds, and the mustard seed.
Luke's shorter version of the sower and its explanation.
Matthew's parallel account of the storm being calmed.

otBackground.note: Seeing without perceiving, hearing without understanding — quoted directly by Jesus to explain His use of parables.
Sailors crying out to God in a storm, who then stills the wind and waves — the same pattern Jesus enacts in v.39.
A great tree sheltering birds in its branches — background imagery echoed directly in the mustard seed parable.

mapCoords.placeName: Sea of Galilee shoreline, near Tabgha

commentary.note: Henry pictures the sower scattering seed indiscriminately, quoting Ecclesiastes 11:1's image of sowing "beside all waters" — the word of God given out to everyone alike, not knowing in advance where it will land or what it will produce. Ministers, he says, are sowers in the same pattern, not judges of the soil.

JFB points out something the text leaves deliberately open: Jesus never actually identifies who the sower is. They read this as intentional — since the seed is the word of God, anyone who scatters that word, in any generation, can be understood as a sower in the same parable, not just Jesus Himself.

Ryle writes with real force about the storm-calming: 'He speaks to the waves, and they submit to His command. He turns the raging storm into a calm with a few words — 'Peace, be still.' The elements knew the voice of their Master, and, like obedient servants, were quiet at once.' No stormy passion, he adds, is too strong for the same Christ to tame.

overview.summary: Teaching from a boat, Jesus tells the parable of the sower, then the lamp, the growing seed, and the mustard seed. That evening he calms a storm on the lake and asks the disciples why they were afraid.
overview.settingLine: The lakeshore, then a boat on the Sea of Galilee.

history.t: Most listeners lived by farming and fishing, so seeds and nets were everyday pictures.
Cold air off the hills can whip up sudden storms on the lake.

customs.t: Farmers scattered seed by hand before plowing it under.
The curved shore works like an amphitheater, carrying a voice across the water.

archaeology.t: A first-century fishing boat found in the lake in 1986 is displayed at Ginosar.
The shoreline near Tabgha has ancient harbor structures.

overview.discussion: The disciples saw Jesus calm the storm and still wondered who He was. What storm do you need Him to speak to?
overview.book: The second Gospel · 16 chapters. A fast-moving account of Jesus as the suffering Servant.
overview.author: Mark
